params.question: Why does gentle scraping of a psoriatic plaque produce pinpoint bleeding (the Auspitz sign)?

answers.text: The silvery parakeratotic scale is firmly adherent and tears the underlying dermis when removed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The scale in psoriasis is actually loosely stacked and weakly adherent — that is why it lifts off as waxy flakes (candle-grease sign). The bleeding arises from the capillary anatomy beneath, not from tearing.

answers.text: Dilated capillaries in the dermal papillae lie just beneath a suprapapillary epidermis thinned to two or three cell layers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In psoriasis, the suprapapillary plate is only two to three cells thick, so even light scraping exposes the dilated capillary loops in the elongated dermal papillae, producing discrete pinpoint haemorrhage.

answers.text: Chronic inflammation produces fragile new blood vessels throughout the full thickness of the plaque

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The bleeding is not from generalised neo-vascularisation. It comes specifically from dilated capillary loops in the dermal papillae that are exposed when the abnormally thin suprapapillary epidermis is breached.

answers.text: The Koebner phenomenon triggers bleeding at any site of minor skin trauma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Koebner phenomenon refers to the appearance of new psoriatic plaques at sites of trauma — it does not explain the Auspitz sign's pinpoint bleeding, which has a structural basis in the thinned epidermis and dilated papillary capillaries.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the plaque architecture: in psoriasis, the suprapapillary epidermis thins to two or three cell layers, and the dermal papillae contain dilated capillaries. Scraping through that thin roof exposes these vessels, producing pinpoint bleeding.

Exactly right — the Auspitz sign is a direct consequence of psoriatic plaque architecture: accelerated turnover thins the suprapapillary epidermis, and dilated papillary capillaries sit immediately beneath it.

params.question: You are demonstrating the Grattage test on a mature psoriatic plaque on a patient's elbow using a glass slide edge. Which sequence of findings confirms a fully positive result?

answers.text: Auspitz sign → terminal film (Büchner sign) → candle-grease sign

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the correct order. The Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding) is the deepest layer and appears last, not first. The test reads the plaque from surface to depth.

answers.text: Candle-grease sign → terminal film (Büchner sign) → Auspitz sign

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Gentle scraping first lifts loosely stacked parakeratotic scale as waxy flakes (candle-grease sign), then exposes a thin glistening membrane (terminal film or Büchner sign), and finally produces pinpoint bleeding from dilated papillary capillaries (Auspitz sign).
The candle-grease sign — silvery flakes lifting off like wax — is the first sign, not the last. The surface scale must be removed before deeper layers are reached.

The Auspitz sign and terminal film are swapped here. After the scale lifts off, the thin glistening membrane (terminal film) must be exposed before pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign) can appear from the capillaries beneath it.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the Grattage test reads the plaque layer by layer from surface to depth. Candle-grease sign (scale lifts as waxy flakes) → terminal film (thin glistening membrane exposed) → Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding from papillary capillaries). Review the plaque architecture in the preceding narration.

Well done. The three signs follow the plaque's architecture from surface to depth: loosely stacked scale → thinned suprapapillary membrane → dilated papillary capillaries. All three must appear in this exact order for a fully positive result.

params.question: A patient presents with papules that show the Koebner phenomenon at a recent scratch mark. Which additional finding would confirm lichen planus rather than psoriasis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Thick silvery-white scale is the hallmark of psoriasis, reflecting parakeratotic keratinocyte build-up from accelerated epidermal turnover. Lichen planus has a smooth, flat-topped surface.

answers.text: Pinpoint bleeding on gentle scraping of the lesion surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pinpoint bleeding is the Auspitz sign — a psoriasis-specific finding caused by dilated capillaries beneath a thinned suprapapillary epidermis. It is absent in lichen planus.

answers.text: Fine white lacy lines (Wickham striae) on the surface of violaceous, flat-topped papules

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Wickham striae — fine white lacy lines from focal thickening of the granular layer — on violaceous, flat-topped (planar) papules are among the most reliable signs of lichen planus. Both conditions Koebnerise, so Koebner alone cannot separate them.

answers.text: Bilateral extensor distribution on the elbows and knees

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Extensor distribution is characteristic of psoriasis. Lichen planus favours flexural sites — the flexor wrists, ankles, and lower back.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember that both psoriasis and lichen planus Koebnerise — Koebner alone cannot distinguish them. Look for the discriminating signs: psoriasis gives silvery scale, Auspitz sign, and extensor distribution; lichen planus gives Wickham striae, violaceous flat-topped papules, and flexural distribution.
Exactly. Both conditions exhibit the Koebner phenomenon, so it cannot separate them. Wickham striae on violaceous flat-topped papules with a flexural distribution point specifically to lichen planus.

params.question: A young woman presents with a pale patch on her hand. On examination, sensation to light touch over the patch is absent, and a Wood's lamp shows no blue-white fluorescence. What is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.text: Vitiligo — autoimmune melanocyte destruction causes depigmented patches

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In vitiligo, sensation is completely normal because the disease targets melanocytes, not nerves. Vitiligo also shows bright chalky blue-white fluorescence under the Wood's lamp. Both findings here point away from vitiligo.

answers.text: Pityriasis versicolor — Malassezia infection producing scaly hypopigmented macules

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pityriasis versicolor shows golden-yellow fluorescence under the Wood's lamp (not absent fluorescence) and has a characteristic scaly surface confirmed by KOH mount showing hyphae and spores. Sensation is preserved.

answers.text: Hansen disease (leprosy) — Mycobacterium leprae damaging peripheral nerves causes an anaesthetic hypopigmented patch

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Absent sensation (the anaesthetic patch) is the hallmark of leprosy and the single most important finding that separates it from vitiligo and other causes. Leprosy patches are hypopigmented (not depigmented) and do not fluoresce under the Wood's lamp.

answers.text: Pityriasis alba — a benign condition causing ill-defined off-white patches

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pityriasis alba typically affects children's faces with ill-defined, slightly scaly off-white patches. Sensation is normal. The presentation here — absent sensation on the hand — does not fit this benign condition.

overallFeedback.feedback: Always apply the three-step assessment on a pale patch: (1) check colour and borders, (2) test sensation, (3) use the Wood's lamp. Absent sensation (anaesthetic patch) is the hallmark of leprosy and the single most important step for excluding it from vitiligo and other causes.

Well identified. The anaesthetic patch is the finding that changes everything — absent sensation means peripheral nerve involvement, pointing to leprosy. This is the critical differential to exclude on every pale patch in India, before any other diagnosis is considered.

params.question: Systemic corticosteroids can be safely used as step-up therapy when topical treatment fails in moderate-to-severe psoriasis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Systemic corticosteroids are absolutely contraindicated in psoriasis. While they may seem effective initially, withdrawal triggers a dangerous rebound into generalised pustular or erythrodermic disease. This contrasts with lichen planus, where systemic steroids are appropriate. For moderate-to-severe psoriasis, the correct systemic options are methotrexate, cyclosporine, or biologics — never corticosteroids.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Systemic corticosteroids are absolutely contraindicated in psoriasis. Although they may initially suppress inflammation, withdrawal triggers rebound into generalised pustular or erythrodermic psoriasis — both life-threatening emergencies. The correct step-up is narrowband UVB phototherapy, followed by methotrexate (with folic acid), cyclosporine, or biologics targeting the IL-23/IL-17 axis for severe disease.
